title: MB0-07599
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, the claimant, who is 42 years old and a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo ("DRC"), is availing herself of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (hereinafter referred to as the IRPA).

In her Personal Information Form (PIF), submitted to the panel on January 10, 2011, and subsequently amended, the claimant alleges that she was married to XXXX XXXX XXXX, a member of the Mouvement de Libération du Congo (MLC) [movement for the liberation of the Congo]. He always campaigned for human rights and denounced human rights violations. Because of her husband's close relationship with XXXX XXXX, soldiers visited the claimant on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, looking for her husband.
They kidnapped the claimant and put her in a prison cell; she was raped before being released with help from two guards.
The claimant left her country for these reasons. She arrived on XXXX XXXX, 2010, and claimed refugee protection on November 24, 2010.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee." The claimant is also not a "person in need of protection" for the following reasons.

The claimant's identity was established to the panel's satisfaction, as a copy of a voter's card issued by DRC authorities was entered in the file by immigration services. The panel concludes that this is an acceptable document establishing identity within the meaning of section 106 of the IRPA.

Essentially, the claimant submitted that she feared the police in her country because she was suspected of hiding her husband, a member of the MLC and friend of XXXX XXXX, who allegedly went to the claimant and her husband's home a few times.

Her husband, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, became a member of the MLC in 2005.1 She stated that, in that capacity, as a "simple member," he collaborated by XXXX leaflets and posters for the MLC, given XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. In 2005-2006, during a presidential election period in the DRC, he allegedly got involved often and for all of the protests that apparently took place during that period.
The claimant also stated that it was the same in 2007 and, subsequently, until 2010.

The claimant testified that her problems began on XXXX XXXX, 2010. That night, her husband called her to explain that his friend, XXXX XXXX, was having problems because he had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant heard nothing else from her husband after that.

On the night of XXXX XXXX to XXXX, 2010, the claimant received a visit from some police officers, who entered her home, searched it and wanted to know where her husband was. They then arrested her and took her to a prison cell, where she was allegedly raped. The claimant testified that she was questioned a few times, and during the questioning, she was asked where her husband was, what the relationship was between her husband and XXXX, and why XXXX acted this way against the government in place.
Each time, the claimant answered that, as a [translation] "housewife," she did not have such political information.
A month later, the claimant managed to flee the prison with help from her sister, who allegedly bribed a guard. She then arranged to leave the DRC and flee to Canada.

The claimant's six children,2 who are still in the country, live with her sister, XXXX, who lives in XXXX XXXX XXXX, which is 30 minutes by car from the house where the claimant was living before she left the DRC. They go to school.

The claimant testified that she talks to her sister on the telephone once or twice a week. She stated that her children are stressed and that they are also wondering where their father could be. The claimant's sister has never told her anything about her-the claimant's-situation in the DRC since she came to Canada. The claimant stated that she is convinced that if her sister had any information, she would have given it to her.

Between 2005, the year the claimant's husband became a member of the MLC, and XXXX 2010, that is, for five years, the claimant's husband had no problems stemming from his membership in the MLC. The claimant testified that if he had had any problems, either he would have told her or she would have figured out that something was not right, because she knew him well.

There is a great deal of documentary evidence on exactions and other problems faced by members of the MLC from 2005 right up until Bemba, the president of the MLC, left the country.3 Although the country was often engaged in a bloody conflict, and the claimant's husband was a member of the MLC, XXXX leaflets and posters, he had no problems for five years.
She was unable to provide any explanation as to why it was only in 2010 that he allegedly had problems, other than the fact that he was friends with XXXX.

The claimant's husband allegedly disappeared in 2010. Moreover, it is within the panel's specialized knowledge, acquired during hearings concerning the DRC, that XXXX, an activist radically opposed to Kabila, died in the XXXX of 2010, after he did indeed XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel raised this specialized knowledge and wanted to know why the authorities would go after her again if she were to return to her country, considering these facts. She stated that she had fled from the prison and that, as a result, someone could be looking for her.

The panel is not satisfied with the claimant's explanations, considering XXXX's death, considering the fact that the claimant's husband had no problems during that entire time, and considering the fact that her children, who still live in the DRC, do not have any problems.
The claimant was unable to establish a serious possibility of persecution on the grounds alleged.

Having considered all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant did not discharge her burden of establishing a serious possibility that she would be persecuted on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should she return to her country.

For these reasons, the panel determines that the refugee protection claimant is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The panel rejects the refugee protection claim filed by XXXX XXXX XXXX.
